 RE             Yangibana Project - Aeromagnetic Prospect/Target Modelling


1  INTRODUCTION
Modelling of magnetic data has been performed over Hastings Technology Metals’ (Hastings) Yangibana
project by Southern Geoscience Consultants (SGC), which is prospective for Rare Earth Elements (REEs),
particularly Neodymium and Praseodymium. The data used was from an aeromagnetic survey flown over
the area in 2016, the details of which are given in Table 1. This data was processed by SGC in 2016.

Table 1. Details of aeromagnetic survey used for magnetic modelling.

Modelling was performed over 5 targets/areas, which are described in Table 2 and shown in Figure 1.

Modelling has also been previously performed by SGC over the Auer North prospect. This area has since
been drill tested and the modelling is reviewed in this memorandum.

Over the Target 5 area, ‘depth filtering’ (a series of upward continuation filters) has been performed in an
attempt to reveal deeper structure/bodies of potential interest.

2  3D INVERSION MODELLING
2.1  Target 1
Three-dimensional unconstrained inversion modelling was performed over the Target 1 feature to derive
information about its depth, size and strength. No other information has been collected over this feature
(mapping, sampling, etc.) prior to this study, is believed to be under cover. An approximately 2.6 x 2.0 km
area of TMI data around the feature was inverted using the UBC v5 code to produce a 3D smooth model of
magnetic susceptibility (SI).

The resultant modelled body (Figure 2) is large, discrete and with a strong magnetic susceptibility. The
shape implies a potential fold structure (synform or antiform) that has been ‘cut’ and offset multiple times
by ENE trending brittle structures (Figure 2). The body appears to have a large depth extent.

Follow-up forward modelling was performed over Target 1 to complement the inversion model and further
understand the structure of the feature (Section 3.2).





Figure 2. Image of magnetic inversion (SI ≥ 0.01) showing an ambiguous fold structure. Interpreted fold axes
annotated with blue dashed lines and interpreted faults annotated with black lines.

2.2  Fraser Fault Zone
The Fraser Fault Zone is a large, structurally complex zone that hosts significant REE mineralisation. The
mineralisation here does not seem to be magnetic itself, however magnetic modelling has been undertaken
to better understand the structure and geometry of the surrounding geology, and by correlation, of the
mineralisation.

Two-dimensional modelling of the Fraser Fault Zone (see Section 3.6) was performed, but was considered
difficult due to the complex structure, variable magnetic signature/Q-factor of units, and strong, variable
regional  field. As a  result, a three-dimensional unconstrained  inversion was performed to better
understand the behaviour of the geology.

Figure 3 shows an image of inversion shells (< -0.002 SI) along with drilling (coloured by Nd2O3+Pr6O11 %,
Blue = 0%, Red = 1%) and an interpreted mineralisation horizon (red). The mineralisation here appears to
be associated with low/non-magnetic bodies and structures that are running through the area.





Figure 3. Inversion over Fraser Fault Zone prospect showing drilling, know mineralisation polygon (red) and
magnetic shells (<-0.002  SI). The mineralisation in this case appears to be associated with the zone of low
magnetism and/or a structure.

3 FORWARD MODELLING
Forward modelling has been carried out over Targets 1, 3, 4, 6 and the Frazer Fault Zone using Potent
software in an attempt to understand the shape, depth and width of bodies that may contain or be linked
to REE mineralisation.

The modelling results are described below and shown in Appendix A.

3.1  Potent Forward Magnetic Modelling
The Potent modelling software calculates the theoretical ‘induced magnetisation’ from simple shapes
(dykes, cylinders, blocks, spheres, etc.) which can be compared to the TMI profiles from field surveys. The
orientation, dimensions, location and magnetic susceptibility of these model bodies can be adjusted until
the calculated response matches the observed response; this process is referred to as ‘forward modelling’.
Limitations of the forward modelling routine include;

    •  There is no unique solution for modelling an observed TMI field, in most scenarios there are more
        variables than there are known parameters. There are trade-offs between different parameters
        that produce similar results. For example, a wider and less magnetic body may produce a similar
       response to a thinner and more magnetic unit.  If some of the parameters can be constrained from
      known geological information (drill-hole data or magnetic susceptibility measurements) then the
       range of solutions can be reduced producing a higher degree of confidence in the modelling.
    •  The induced magnetic field decreases strongly with distance.  This means that the magnetic
        material closest to the magnetometer has the strongest response and generally produces better
       constrained models than magnetic material that is further from the sensor. For ground or airborne
      TMI surveys, the top of the magnetic bodies are easier to model than the deeper extents.  For
       borehole surveys, magnetic material closer to the drillhole is easier to model than the magnetic
        material far from the drill hole.
    •   Multiple magnetic bodies that are closer to each other than their distance to the magnetometer
       cannot be resolved as separate sources – their magnetic fields will superimpose to look like that of
       a single magnetic body.  What has been modelled as a single magnetic body may actually be
      composed of a number of smaller and closely spaced bodies.
    •  When modelling magnetic bodies the thickness and susceptibility values cannot be resolved
         individually. The induced magnetic field will be a product of the volume of magnetic material (i.e.
        thickness x magnetic susceptibility) such that a 10m thick body with susceptibility of 1.0 SI will
       produce the same result as a 20m thick body of 0.5 SI.
    •   Potent forward modelling uses simple shapes to model what can be very complex geological
        scenarios. The best results are achieved where simple geology is modelled using TMI profiles that
       are close to being perpendicular to the dominant strike direction. Modelling TMI profiles that are
       oblique or parallel to strike can be very difficult, particularly where geology is very complex.
    •  The observed TMI response can be affected by remanent magnetisation, anisotropic magnetisation
       or demagnetisation which are difficult to quantify and account for. These effects distort the TMI
       anomaly (from the induced magnetisation) and will introduce errors into the modelling efforts.
    •  Forward modelling is often referred to as 2D modelling. The models generated apply only to the
         profile being modelled.  Data from nearby lines can be used to help constrain the orientation
         (strike, dip, plunge, length) of the model bodies, in which case the modelling is sometimes referred
        to as 2.5 D modelling. The models generated for each profile are valid only for that data on that
         profile; the results should not be extrapolated too far away from the modelled data.

In general the magnetic modelling can be improved by constraining parameters with known information
and by recording magnetic profiles closer to the magnetic source rocks. For the modelling of airborne TMI
data this means the modelling results can be improved by recording ground or borehole TMI profiles and
using drilling data to constrain the dimensions and magnetic susceptibility of the magnetic model bodies.

An example of a 2D model section is shown below in Figure 4. For each model profile the TMI (top panel)
and the two derivatives TMI_dz (first vertical derivative of TMI – second panel) and Manalytic (analytic
signal of TMI – third panel) have been modelled. The derivatives help to isolate the response of closely
spaced magnetic bodies and identify the edges of shallow targets. The observed profiles are shown in blue
and the calculated profiles in red. The lowest panel on each profile shows the cross section of the profile
with the relevant model bodies and drill holes projected onto the section. The AMAG survey flight path is
shown as a green trace and the terrain as a brown trace (all RL positions are relative to the aircraft GPS
heights). The model body cross sections are filled in and the ends are projected onto the section (near side
is solid and the far side is dashed). The cross section direction is labelled in the lower right-hand corner
(“AZ=89.9 deg”)

3.2  Target 1
Forward modelling was carried out on three flight lines over the Target 1 feature to complement the 3D
inversion – Lines 110370, 110430 and 110540. Three dyke-like bodies were used to model the feature.
Modelling implies the body could represent a magnetic antiform with two or more folded magnetic
horizons, with vertically to steeply dipping limbs.

3.3  Target 3
Target 3 comprises the (possibly mineralised) northern extension of the Auer magnetic trend. Survey lines
in this area are angled parallel to the trend, with no perpendicular tie lines crossing directly over the
features of interest. As a result, the data across multiple parallel survey lines (109210 to 109310) was
extracted for modelling. This had the disadvantage that station spacing was limited to line spacing (25m),
but was seen as better than attempting to model gridded data, which was smoothed and could not be
modelled in conjunction with the parallel line data in Potent.

Modelling produced two relatively thin (15-20m), steeply dipping bodies with steep dips, although the dips
are ambiguous given the low sample spacing.

3.4  Target 4
Target 4 is similar to Target 3 in that it is the possible southern extension of the Auer magnetic trend.
Unlike Target 3, there were perpendicular tie lines crossing directly over the features of interest in this
area. Lines 109360, 109400, 190170 and 190190 were utilised in the modelling.

Modelling produced two relatively steeply dipping bodies, 20-30 metres wide and plunging to the south.
Surrounding and ‘deeper’ magnetic features were also modelled, including one body which was given a
negative magnetic susceptibility in order to fit the regional signal.

3.5  Target 6
Target 6 is a thin magnetic anomaly coincident with an anomalous surface sample. Lines 109670 and
190340 have been used for modelling.

Magnetic modelling shows the body to be extremely thin, shallow and strongly magnetic – possibly with an
element of remanence. ‘Inversion’ of the polygon within Potent produced an unrealistic model located
above the surface. Review of the magnetic image leads belief that the body is possibly a shallow, magnetic
palaeochannel feature. It is coincident with modern drainage when viewed in conjunction with satellite
imagery.

3.6  Fraser Fault Zone
Two-dimensional modelling was initially performed at the Fraser Fault zone to determine depths, dips and
geometries of units in the target area. Lines 110780, 110860, 110970 and 190430 were used for modelling.

Due to the strong regional/variation in basement magnetism, line-to-line modelling was difficult and where
it was difficult to directly fit the TMI data, modelling focussed on the TMI 1VD data in order to determine
the geometries of the units.

4  AUER FORWARD MODELLING REVIEW
The Auer and Auer North forward models produced by SGC in 2016 have been compared against drilling
results and the derived mineralisation polygon (Figure 5).

Drilling shows the width of the mineralisation to be thin (<3 metres), whereas the polygons of widths of 5
and 20 metres were modelled in order to fit this data. This could reflect that the magnetic halo around the
mineralisation is wider than the mineralisation itself.

The mineralisation polygon supplied by Hastings shows the mineralisation to be reaching surface, and the
dip to be steeper than the model. The magnetic models were located at approximately 50 to 80 metres
depth – although the modelling could be better constrained now,  it  is  likely the top layer of the
mineralisation has been oxidised by weathering and has therefore lost magnetism (as magnetite oxidises to
hematite). The dips of the magnetic model tend to reflect a best/average estimate which was not too far
from reality in this instance.





Figure 5. Comparison of 5m-wide magnetic models (blue), drilling and mineralisation polygon (red). Drilling
coloured with Nd2O3+Pr6O11 % (Blue = 0%, Red = 1%).





© 2018 Southern Geoscience Consultants Pty Ltd                                                                 8

5  DEPTH FILTERING
Filtering of the magnetic data was undertaken in order to suppress high frequency/noisy surface signal with
the aim of revealing deeper components in the Target 5 area of interest (ref. Figure 1). A series of upward-
continuation filters were applied to the RTP data, which simulate the data being collected further away
from the source (e.g. a 20 metre upward-continuation filter simulates the data being collected from 20
metres higher; since the original data was collected at 30 metres terrain clearance, this would be a virtual
terrain clearance of 50 metres).

Upward continuation filters of 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 metres were performed on the RTP data, and a first
vertical derivative was then applied to highlight structural features (Figure 6). With each increase in
continuation, shorter wavelength features (e.g. shallow, high magnetic) are merged/suppressed and longer
wavelength features are accentuated to highlight deeper and more major structures and geometries. This
information can then be used to ‘zone in’ to areas of interest.

A number of candidate larger, deeper magnetic bodies have been highlighted by this depth filtering (50-
100m upward continuation imagery) and should be assessed from a geological perspective as to
exploration interest (Figure 7).

6  CONCLUSIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS
Forward and inversion modelling has been undertaken on magnetic data collected over Hastings’
Yangibana project in 2016 in order to characterise prospects based on magnetic signature before follow-up
work is performed.
It is believed that Target 1 represents a priority target worthy of more detailed investigation given the
2D/3D modelling that has been completed, this local magnetic body has a differing/stronger signature to
other magnetic units in the local vicinity and is bounded by a major ~WNW-ESE structure along  it’s
southern margin.  It is believed that this magnetic unit is under thin cover. Optimised drill testing of both
limbs of this Target 1 magnetic unit is recommended.
Targets 3 and 4 represent steeply dipping, relatively thin magnetic units of a similar nature to the
Auer/Auer North prospects, and drill testing of both targets is recommended.
Target 6 appears to be representative of a shallow, magnetic paleochannel and follow up work such as
shallow drill testing is recommended.
Both forward and inversion modelling has been performed at the Fraser Fault Zone prospect due to the
complexity of the magnetic signal. These models should be integrated with the existing drilling and
geological models in increase understanding and generate new drill targets.
The Auer forward modelling performed in 2016 was reviewed against new drill results and a mineralisation
outline. The model  is slightly shallower dipping and slightly thicker, but otherwise provides a good
estimation of the behaviour of magnetic mineralisation horizon and is a successful proof-of-concept for
future modelling studies in this project.
Depth filtering for the broader Target 5 area has defined a number of deeper/broader magnetic anomaly
centres which should be assessed in more detail from a geological perspective/spatial context given the
mapped structure/geology.  Local 3D inversion of priority deeper anomalism deemed to be of geological
interest at Target 5 is recommended to ascertain potential source depths/geometries.
